nameStory: The interrupted turbonille gets its name from the distinctive interrupted pattern on its shell, where the usual spiral ridges or decorative lines appear broken or discontinuous. The word 'turbonille' comes from the Latin 'turbo' meaning spinning top, referring to the shell's elongated, cone-like shape that resembles a tiny spinning top.
description: The interrupted turbonille is a tiny sea snail that lives in New England's coastal waters. This marine gastropod (belly-footed mollusk) has an elongated, cone-shaped shell that spirals to a pointed tip. Like other pyramid snails in its family, it's quite small and easy to overlook among beach debris. These little snails are parasites that feed on other marine organisms by inserting a feeding tube into their hosts.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, narrow cone shape that tapers to a sharp point, resembling a tiny ice cream cone or spinning top

idTips.label: Interrupted Pattern
idTips.description: Look for broken or discontinuous lines, ridges, or spiral patterns on the shell surface that appear to start and stop rather than flow continuously

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, easily fitting on your fingernail with room to spare - you'll need good eyes or a magnifying glass to see details clearly

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface when fresh, feeling almost porcelain-like to the touch if you can handle one carefully

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Typically whitish, cream, or pale yellow coloration, sometimes with a subtle translucent quality

habitat: Found in New England's marine environments, particularly in sandy or muddy coastal areas where their host organisms live. Look for empty shells washed up on beaches, especially in wrack lines (piles of seaweed and debris left by tides) along protected shores and bays. Living specimens are typically found in shallow subtidal zones where they can access their preferred hosts.

seasonality.spring: Shell collecting is excellent as winter storms wash up specimens. Look for tiny shells mixed in with beach wrack and other marine debris.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding both living specimens in tide pools and fresh shells on beaches. Warm weather makes beach combing more pleasant for detailed searching.
seasonality.fall: Continued good shell hunting as autumn storms churn up the seafloor. Check beaches after storm systems pass through the area.
seasonality.winter: Harsh weather limits collecting opportunities, but major storms can deposit unusual specimens. Bundle up and check beaches after nor'easters.

funFact: Despite being tiny, interrupted turbonilles are actually vampires of the sea - they use a needle-like feeding tube called a proboscis to pierce other marine animals and suck out their body fluids, making them some of the smallest parasitic predators in New England waters!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pyramid snails, but the interrupted pattern on the shell is the key distinguishing feature. Remember: 'interrupted lines, interrupted turbonille' - look for those broken spiral patterns rather than smooth, continuous ridges.
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'Pyramidellidae' refers to the pyramid-like shell shape, but don't expect to see actual pyramid snails easily - most are parasitic and quite secretive in their habits. What you'll typically find are empty shells rather than living animals.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Bush's turbonille (Turbonilla bushiana), the interrupted turbonille shows those distinctive broken or discontinuous patterns on its shell surface. Bush's turbonille tends to have more regular, continuous spiral ridges or smoother shell surfaces. Both are extremely small pyramid snails, but focus on the shell pattern - continuous versus interrupted - to tell them apart.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bush's Turbonille differs from its relative the Interrupted Turbonille by having a smoother shell surface without the distinctive bands or interruptions that give the latter species its name.
